segments.text: Learning is a relatively lasting change in behaviour or knowledge that comes from experience. Memory refers to the processes through which information is encoded, retained and later retrieved. The two areas are closely connected: learning creates new information or behaviour, while memory helps preserve and use it.
This is one of the most scoring units when concepts are kept distinct. Most mistakes come from mixing classical conditioning, operant conditioning, reinforcement and punishment.

items.text: Classical conditioning

: Classical conditioning involves learning an association between stimuli. A previously neutral stimulus can come to trigger a response after repeated pairing with a stimulus that naturally produces that response.
Operant conditioning
: Operant conditioning involves learning from the consequences of behaviour. Behaviours followed by reinforcing consequences become more likely, while punishment is intended to reduce behaviour.
Reinforcement and punishment

: Positive means adding something; negative means removing something. Reinforcement increases behaviour; punishment decreases behaviour. Therefore negative reinforcement is not punishment: it strengthens behaviour by removing an unpleasant condition.
Extinction and discrimination

: Extinction refers to weakening of a learned response when the relevant reinforcement or pairing is no longer maintained. Discrimination means learning to respond differently to different stimuli or situations.
Observational learning
: People can learn by observing others and the consequences others experience. Attention, memory, ability to reproduce the behaviour and motivation all matter.
Memory process
: A practical memory model uses encoding, storage and retrieval. Memory is not a single box; different systems handle information over different timescales and for different functions.
Forgetting

: Forgetting may result from weak encoding, interference, retrieval failure, decay-like processes in some conditions, or other mechanisms. A good answer distinguishes theories instead of naming them without explanation.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

items.text: Core mechanism

: In classical conditioning, an organism learns that one stimulus predicts another. A neutral cue becomes a conditioned stimulus after repeated pairing with an unconditioned stimulus, and it can then evoke a conditioned response.
Acquisition

: Acquisition is the period in which the conditioned relationship is learned. Learning is stronger when the conditioned stimulus reliably predicts the unconditioned stimulus rather than merely appearing near it.
Extinction

: If the conditioned stimulus repeatedly appears without the expected unconditioned stimulus, the conditioned response usually weakens. Extinction is new learning rather than simple erasure, which helps explain spontaneous recovery after time has passed.
Generalization and discrimination

: Generalization occurs when similar stimuli evoke a learned response; discrimination occurs when the learner distinguishes the relevant cue from other cues. Both processes are important in fear, preferences and everyday prediction.
Reinforcement

: A consequence is reinforcing if it increases the future probability of the behaviour it follows. Positive reinforcement adds a desirable event; negative reinforcement removes or prevents an aversive event. The words positive and negative mean adding and removing, not good and bad.
Punishment

: Punishment aims to reduce behaviour. Positive punishment adds an aversive consequence, while negative punishment removes a valued stimulus or opportunity. Punishment may suppress behaviour without teaching a better alternative and can have unwanted emotional or avoidance effects.
Shaping
: Complex behaviours can be built by reinforcing successive approximations to the desired behaviour. Shaping illustrates that learning can be gradual rather than all-or-none.
Schedules of reinforcement

: Continuous reinforcement is useful during acquisition, while intermittent schedules can produce persistent responding. Ratio schedules depend on number of responses; interval schedules depend on time. Variable schedules are often resistant to extinction because reinforcement is unpredictable.
Observational learning

: Bandura's work demonstrated that people can acquire behavioural patterns by observing models. Attention, retention, ability to reproduce the act and motivation influence whether observed behaviour is later performed.
Vicarious consequences
: People can learn from what happens to others rather than experiencing every consequence directly. This is important in families, classrooms, media and workplaces.
Cognitive maps and expectations

: Learning can include internal representations and expectations. Tolman's maze research was historically important because it challenged the idea that all learning can be reduced to immediately reinforced stimulus-response links.
Encoding
: Encoding transforms information into a form that can be represented in memory. Attention and meaningful elaboration usually improve encoding more than passive repetition.
Working memory

: Working memory temporarily maintains and manipulates information needed for tasks such as mental arithmetic, comprehension and planning. It is limited, which is why chunking and external notes can reduce cognitive load.
Long-term memory

: Long-term memory includes declarative forms such as episodic and semantic memory and nondeclarative forms such as procedural skills and some conditioned responses. These systems rely partly on different neural processes.
Retrieval

: Remembering depends on effective retrieval cues. Context and state can influence access to stored information, and testing oneself can improve later retrieval more effectively than repeated rereading.

blocks.text: Why forgetting occurs and what improves retention

items.text: Encoding failure
: Some apparent forgetting reflects information that was never encoded deeply enough. Seeing an object repeatedly does not guarantee memory for its details if attention was never directed to them.
Interference

: Proactive interference occurs when older learning disrupts newer information; retroactive interference occurs when newer learning disrupts older information. Similar material often produces more interference.
Retrieval failure
: Information may be stored but temporarily inaccessible because effective cues are absent. Recognition can therefore be easier than free recall.
Reconstructive memory
: Memory is not a literal recording. People reconstruct past events using stored fragments, schemas and later information. This is central to understanding eyewitness errors.
Evidence-based study practice
: Spacing study over time, retrieval practice, elaboration, interleaving where appropriate and adequate sleep are more defensible strategies than relying on last-minute repetition alone.

Make a 2 × 2 table for positive/negative reinforcement and positive/negative punishment.
Draw a simple memory flow: encoding → storage → retrieval.
Practise application questions involving study habits, classroom learning, advertising, fear or habit formation.

rows: Avoid this error The most common error is calling negative reinforcement “punishment.” Remember: reinforcement always increases the future probability of a behaviour.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Begin with definitions, compare classical and operant conditioning, explain reinforcement/punishment, add observational learning, then move to memory systems, processes and forgetting. A comparison table can make the answer very clear.
• Operant conditioning links behaviour with consequences.
• Reinforcement strengthens behaviour; punishment attempts to weaken it.
• Memory involves encoding, storage and retrieval.
• Observational learning does not require the observer to receive direct reinforcement every time.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
